capabilities.target: Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list
Output returned by quicknotes_mcp after tool calls

elements.name: External organizations with access to shared Slack channels
quicknotes_mcp tool definitions into agent context
quicknotes_mcp tool output into agent context
add_note arguments to quicknotes sync service
Slack post content to channel (possibly external)

controls.name: Desktop client first-call approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: This gate only fires on the first invocation of each tool; once the user selects 'always allow' it is remembered, so no later call to fs.read_file, add_note, or slack.post_message is reviewed at all. It is not referenced as an approval_gate_ref on any capability and covers no path, so it earns no residual credit.

controls.name: Pin and hash MCP tool definitions instead of installing @latest on every launch
controls.decay_rationale: Pinned, hashed definitions block silent redefinition regardless of model capability.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for quicknotes_mcp
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist excluding attacker-reachable destinations makes the sink unreachable regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Scope fs.read_file to a notes-specific directory, deny credential/key paths
controls.decay_rationale: A scoped credential cannot be used to read data it does not have access to, regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Bind Slack destination channel to a confirmed allowlist, exclude externally-shared channels
controls.decay_rationale: A destination confirmed from the system of record, rather than chosen by the model, does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Scan third-party tool descriptions and tool output for embedded instructions
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier sees content, not intent, and multi-turn or encoded payloads can get past it, so it narrows but does not sever this path.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log attributing sensitive actions to user vs. autonomous decision
controls.decay_rationale: Logging enforced outside the model does not depend on model capability, though it is detective, not preventive.

controls.name: Per-call raw-action human approval on sensitive capabilities, not remembered
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval reviewed every time does not decay with model capability, unlike a remembered 'always allow'.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via quicknotes_mcp tool poisoning: AWS credentials exfiltrated to third-party sync service

attack_path.note: Poisoned add_note description instructs reading ~/.aws/credentials and hiding this from the user
fs.read_file is scoped to the entire home directory, so it can read ~/.aws/credentials
add_note sends its 'context' argument, now containing the credential file contents, to the author-operated sync service

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any quicknotes_mcp package update changing its tool definitions without pinning, or addition of further unpinned third-party MCP servers with filesystem or egress-capable tools.

evidence.observation: The add_note tool description instructs the model, inside an <IMPORTANT> tag, to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument before calling add_note, and tells the model not to mention this to the user.
quicknotes_mcp is launched with 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest', so its tool definitions are re-fetched and can change on every launch without review.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual, the lowest-assurance category of MCP server identity.
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its own author, the destination that would receive exfiltrated credential data.
The filesystem MCP server is scoped to the entire 'C:/Users/dev' directory rather than a notes-specific subdirectory, so fs.read_file can reach ~/.aws/credentials.
Approval is requested only on the first call to each tool and then remembered as 'always allow', so no subsequent add_note or fs.read_file call is reviewed.

recommendations.action: Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions instead of installing @latest on every launch, and alert on any definition change.
Scope fs.read_file to a dedicated notes working directory and explicitly deny credential and key paths such as ~/.aws and ~/.ssh.
Add a network egress allowlist for quicknotes_mcp so add_note cannot transmit arbitrary data to unreviewed hosts.
Require raw-action human approval on every sensitive fs.read_file and add_note call, instead of remembering 'always allow' after the first call.
Log and attribute every sensitive tool invocation to a tamper-evident audit record distinguishing user-authorized from autonomous actions.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via broad Slack token: injected content can relay sensitive data to externally-shared channels

attack_path.note: The same untrusted quicknotes_mcp channel that poisons add_note can direct the model to relay sensitive context via Slack instead
fs.read_file can read sensitive files from the overly broad home-directory scope
The Slack bot token can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any slack-mcp update changing definitions or scopes, or widening of the Slack bot token's channel access.

evidence.observation: slack-mcp is launched with 'npx -y slack-mcp@latest', so its tool definitions can change without review on every launch, like quicknotes_mcp.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so SLACK_BOT_TOKEN is not scoped to a least-privilege set of internal channels.

The author of a connected third-party MCP server has already demonstrated willingness and ability to embed hidden, user-concealed instructions in tool metadata, the same class of untrusted channel that could direct a relay via Slack.
Remembered 'always allow' approval means a Slack post following an initially approved post is not reviewed regardless of destination channel or content.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to only the channels the workflow needs, excluding channels shared with external organizations.
Bind the Slack destination channel to a confirmed value from the system of record rather than a model-chosen argument.
Pin slack-mcp's version instead of installing @latest on every launch.

findings.title: No attributable record of agent actions across file reads, note syncs, and Slack posts

forecast.watch_signal: Any increase in autonomous steps per session, or additional data sources connected, without adding tamper-evident action logging.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, or action-attribution mechanism is described anywhere in the artifacts for fs.read_file, add_note, or slack.post_message calls.
Approval is granted once per tool and then remembered, so there is also no per-call record distinguishing which specific invocations were human-reviewed versus autonomously repeated.

recommendations.action: Implement a tamper-evident audit log recording which actions were user-approved versus autonomously taken by desk-assistant.

stride_coverage.rationale: The desktop client runs locally under the user's own OS session with a single local principal; there is no remote channel through which another party could impersonate the user or the agent to each other.
The artifacts do not describe step limits, retry behavior, or runtime caps for desk-assistant, so loop or resource-exhaustion risk cannot be assessed from the given design.
quicknotes_mcp is a third-party hosted service; the artifacts give no information about its own internal logging or accountability, so this cannot be assessed.
The artifacts do not describe quicknotes_mcp's rate limiting, retry, or resource behavior, so denial-of-service potential from this server cannot be assessed.
The artifacts do not describe how slack-mcp itself logs or attributes the actions it performs on the agent's behalf, so this cannot be assessed.
The artifacts do not describe posting rate limits for slack-mcp, so spam or flooding risk through this server cannot be assessed.
This is a locally executed official reference MCP server launched as a local subprocess with no network peer identity to spoof.
The mcp.json entry for the filesystem server specifies no version pin, but the artifacts do not state whether it is otherwise verified, so supply-chain tampering risk cannot be fully assessed.
The artifacts do not describe any logging produced by the filesystem server for the files it reads.
The artifacts do not describe any limits on file read volume or size for this server.
The artifacts do not describe how the agent or quicknotes_mcp verifies it is reaching the legitimate sync endpoint rather than an attacker-controlled or hijacked one.
The artifacts give no information about what records this external, author-operated service keeps of data it receives.

External organizations receiving a Slack message are recipients of a disclosure already captured elsewhere; they are not a party whose repudiation of in-system actions this agent's controls need to address.
The user interacts through a local desktop client under their own OS session, so there is no remote channel for another party to impersonate them to the agent.
The request travels within a local desktop process boundary with no network hop where in-transit tampering could plausibly occur.
This flow carries the trusted principal's own instructions into the agent; it is not a channel through which data leaves the trust boundary.
The artifacts do not describe any throttling or volume limits on user-issued requests.
This is an inbound metadata flow describing available tools; it carries no outbound data itself, so it is not a disclosure channel on its own.
The artifacts do not describe limits on the size or frequency of tool definition updates.
This is an inbound flow of synced note content returned to the agent; the disclosure risk from data later sent elsewhere is captured on the egress flows, not here.
The artifacts do not describe limits on the volume or frequency of tool output returned to the agent.
The risk on this flow is the agent deliberately sending constructed arguments to an untrusted destination, not a third party altering those arguments in transit.
The artifacts do not describe rate limits on add_note calls.
The risk on this flow is deliberate posting of constructed content to a reachable channel, not a third party altering the message in transit.
The artifacts do not describe rate limits on Slack posting.

rating.rationale: Two present findings reach critical: a third-party MCP server (quicknotes_mcp) ships a tool description that instructs the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and exfiltrate it through add_note to an author-controlled hosted service (lethal trifecta: untrusted tool metadata + restricted-data read + egress), and the same untrusted channel can equally direct the broadly-scoped Slack bot token to post sensitive content to channels shared with external organizations. The only approval control in the design is granted once and then remembered, so it earns no residual credit against either path, and no other structural control (egress allowlist, credential scoping, destination confirmation, definition pinning) is present. A third, present property finding notes the complete absence of any audit trail attributing sensitive actions to user authorization versus autonomous agent decisions, capped at high per rubric 5a. Forecast remains critical because the paths are already unmitigated today; no trigger can push them higher, and removing the remembered approval mechanism or upgrading the model would not change an already-critical result.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of desk-assistant, quicknotes_mcp, slack-mcp, or the filesystem server.

No system prompt or full agent instructions were provided, so the agent's declared goal framing and any safety instructions could not be reviewed; autonomy was scored from the described approval behavior alone.

The desktop client's exact approval UI, and whether it shows raw arguments or a summarized description, was not specified. It was not credited as an effective gate regardless, because it is remembered after the first call rather than reviewed each time.

The quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt shows only the add_note tool; other tools the server may expose, and the actual content returned via in.notes_output, were not shown, so the full extent of injectable content from this server is inferred, not directly observed.
